questions.statement: Choose the correct form of the verb to complete the sentence: "Every morning, I _______ my breakfast at 7:30 AM."
questions.context: Martina vive en Buenos Aires y describe su rutina diaria a un amigo.

options.feedback: Esta opción usa el gerundio, que requiere un verbo auxiliar (como 'am') y no se usa para rutinas generales en presente simple.
¡Correcto! Usamos el presente simple en infinitivo (sin 's') para la primera persona del singular (I) al hablar de rutinas.
Esta forma se usa para la tercera persona del singular (he, she, it), no para 'I'.
Este es el pasado simple del verbo 'eat', pero la oración describe una rutina presente ("Every morning").

questions.explanation:
Para expresar rutinas y hábitos en presente simple con el pronombre "I", debés usar la forma base del verbo. En este caso, "eat" es la opción correcta porque Martina está describiendo algo que hace todos los días en la Ciudad de Buenos Aires.

---

questions.statement: Complete the sentence using the Present Continuous: "Wait a second, Facundo can't talk right now. He _______ a shower."
questions.context: Facundo está en Córdoba y está hablando por teléfono sobre lo que está haciendo en este preciso momento.

options.feedback: El presente simple indica hábito, pero la frase "right now" requiere una acción en progreso.
Falta el verbo auxiliar 'is' para formar el presente continuo correctamente.
¡Excelente! El presente continuo se forma con 'is' + verbo con '-ing' para acciones que ocurren en el momento.
'Are' se usa con you, we y they, pero no con 'he'.

questions.explanation:
Cuando querés describir una acción que está pasando justo ahora (como Facundo bañándose), tenés que usar el presente continuo. Recordá que la estructura es: Sujeto + am/is/are + verbo con -ing. Como el sujeto es "He", corresponde usar "is having".

---

questions.statement: Which sentence is grammatically correct for a permanent truth or a natural fact?
questions.context: Un grupo de turistas visita las Cataratas del Iguazú y observa el clima.

options.text: The water is falling very fast today.
options.feedback: Aunque es gramaticalmente correcta, describe una situación específica de hoy, no necesariamente una verdad permanente.

options.text: Iguazu Falls attracts thousands of tourists every year.
options.feedback: ¡Muy bien! El presente simple se usa para hechos permanentes o verdades generales.

options.text: The sun is shining in Misiones every day.
options.feedback: El presente continuo no se usa para acciones que ocurren "todos los días" como una regla general.

options.text: Tourists visiting the park right now.
options.feedback: A esta oración le falta el verbo auxiliar 'are' para ser un presente continuo correcto.

questions.explanation:
El presente simple es el tiempo verbal que usamos para hablar de hechos que no cambian o situaciones permanentes. En este ejemplo, el hecho de que las Cataratas atraen turistas es una constante, por lo que usamos "attracts" (con 's' porque Iguazu Falls funciona como un sujeto singular en este contexto de lugar).

---

questions.statement: Complete the text with the correct tenses: "Normally, I _______ (study) at the university, but this week I _______ (visit) some vineyards in Mendoza."
questions.context: Lucía está comparando sus actividades habituales con lo que está haciendo hoy por las vacaciones en Mendoza.

options.feedback: La segunda parte de la oración describe una situación temporal ("this week"), por lo que requiere presente continuo.
La primera parte describe una rutina normal, por lo que debería estar en presente simple.
¡Correcto! Usás presente simple para lo habitual ("normally") y presente continuo para lo temporal ("this week").
Faltan los verbos auxiliares necesarios para formar los tiempos correctamente.

questions.explanation:
En inglés, es fundamental distinguir entre lo que hacés siempre (rutina) y lo que estás haciendo por un tiempo limitado. Lucía usa el presente simple ("study") para su vida normal y el presente continuo ("am visiting") para su viaje actual a Mendoza.

---

questions.statement: In sports commentaries, we often use the Present Simple for quick actions. Choose the correct option: "Messi _______ the ball, _______ the defender, and scores!"
questions.context: Un periodista deportivo está relatando un partido de fútbol en el Monumental.

options.feedback: El presente continuo haría que el relato suene muy lento para una acción rápida de fútbol.
¡Exacto! El presente simple se usa en relatos deportivos para dar dinamismo a las acciones sucesivas.
Falta la 's' de la tercera persona del singular para el sujeto 'Messi'.
Estas formas solas no funcionan como verbos principales conjugados en la oración.

questions.explanation:
Cuando relatás un partido, como uno en la cancha de River, usás el presente simple para las acciones rápidas que se suceden una tras otra. Acordate de agregar la "s" porque el sujeto es Messi (él).

---

questions.statement: Which question is correctly formed to ask about an action happening now?
questions.context: Martina le pregunta a su hermano sobre sus planes inmediatos mientras están en Rosario.

options.text: Do you listen to music now?
options.feedback: "Do you listen" se usa para hábitos, no para preguntar qué está haciendo alguien en este momento.
En el presente continuo, el verbo principal debe terminar en -ing.
¡Perfecto! La estructura para preguntas en presente continuo es: Am/Is/Are + sujeto + verbo-ing?
El auxiliar 'Is' no concuerda con el pronombre 'you'.

questions.explanation:
Para preguntarle a alguien qué está haciendo en el momento, tenés que usar la inversión del verbo "to be" y el gerundio (-ing). Si estás en Rosario y querés saber qué hace tu amigo, la forma correcta es "Are you listening...?".

---

questions.statement: Some verbs are usually NOT used in the continuous form. Choose the correct sentence:
questions.context: Un estudiante analiza el uso de verbos estáticos (stative verbs) en una descripción de La Plata.

options.text: I am knowing the history of La Plata very well.
options.feedback: El verbo 'know' es estático; describe un estado mental y no suele usarse en continuo.

options.text: I know the history of La Plata very well.
options.feedback: ¡Muy bien! Los verbos de pensamiento o estado como 'know' se usan preferentemente en presente simple.

options.text: I am having a big house in the city center. (meaning possession)
options.feedback: Cuando 'have' significa poseer, no se usa en la forma continua.
Aunque se escucha a veces, 'taste' como percepción de estado suele ir en presente simple: "tastes great".

questions.explanation:
Hay verbos que expresan estados, no acciones físicas, como "know", "love" o "understand". Estos verbos casi nunca llevan -ing. Por eso, aunque estés pensando en algo ahora, decís "I know" y no "I am knowing".

---

questions.statement: The Present Simple can be used for future events that are part of a timetable. Which sentence reflects this?
questions.context: Dos amigos discuten sobre el uso del presente para hablar del futuro cercano (horarios programados).

options.text: I am going to the cinema tomorrow.
options.feedback: Esto es una intención o plan personal, no un horario fijo oficial.

options.text: The bus to Mar del Plata leaves at 10 PM tonight.
options.feedback: ¡Exacto! Usamos el presente simple para transportes o eventos con horarios fijos, incluso si son en el futuro.

options.text: I will leave for Mar del Plata later.
options.feedback: Esto es una decisión espontánea o predicción usando 'will', no el uso del presente simple para horarios.

options.text: The bus is leaving right now.
options.feedback: Esto describe la acción que está pasando en este instante, no un horario programado a futuro.

questions.explanation:
Fijate que a veces el presente simple se "disfraza" de futuro. Si estás en Retiro esperando un micro, podés decir "The bus leaves at..." porque es un horario oficial del transporte. Es una regla muy común para trenes, aviones y micros en Argentina.

---

questions.statement:
What is the difference between these two sentences?
1. I think Bariloche is beautiful.
2. I am thinking about moving to Bariloche.
questions.context: Analizando la diferencia de significado del verbo "think" según el tiempo verbal.

options.text: There is no difference; both are about the present.
options.feedback: Sí hay diferencia; el tiempo verbal cambia el sentido del verbo 'think'.

options.text: Sentence 1 is an opinion (state); sentence 2 is a mental process (action).
options.feedback: ¡Excelente análisis! 'Think' como opinión es estático, como proceso mental es una acción.

options.text: Sentence 1 is a habit; sentence 2 is a permanent truth.
options.feedback: Ninguna de las dos describe un hábito o una verdad universal en ese sentido.

options.text: Sentence 1 is incorrect because 'think' should always be in continuous.
options.feedback: Al contrario, 'think' como opinión suele ser simple.

questions.explanation:
El verbo "think" es especial. Si lo usás para dar tu opinión (lo que creés), va en presente simple ("I think"). Pero si hablás de que estás procesando una idea en tu cabeza en este momento, podés usar el continuo ("I am thinking"). ¡Ojo con esa distinción!

---

questions.statement: Evaluate the use of "always" in this sentence: "You are always losing your SUBE card!" What does the speaker want to express?
questions.context: Un debate sobre el uso del Present Continuous para expresar molestia con adverbios como "always".

options.text: A regular habit that happens every day.
options.feedback: Si fuera un hábito neutral, se usaría presente simple: "You always lose...".

options.text: Annoyance or irritation about a repeated action.
options.feedback: ¡Correcto! El presente continuo con 'always' se usa para quejarse de algo que pasa con demasiada frecuencia.

options.text: A scheduled event in the future.
options.feedback: No tiene nada que ver con horarios o calendarios.

options.text: A compliment about the person's memory.
options.feedback: Claramente es una crítica por perder la tarjeta de transporte.

questions.explanation:
Aunque "always" suele ir con el presente simple, cuando lo combinás con el presente continuo ("You are always..."), estás expresando que algo te irrita o te molesta. Es como decir: "¡Che, siempre estás perdiendo la SUBE!".

---

questions.statement: Find the error in this paragraph: "The tourism industry in Salta grows every year. Currently, more and more people are visit the Northwest."
questions.context: Revisión de un texto sobre la economía regional en Salta.

options.text: 'grows' should be 'is growing' because it's happening now.
options.feedback: 'Grows' es correcto para una tendencia anual general.
¡Exacto! El presente continuo para tendencias actuales requiere el gerundio (-ing).

options.text: 'every year' cannot be used with the Present Simple.
options.feedback: Al revés, es una de las expresiones de tiempo más comunes para el presente simple.

options.text: There are no errors in the paragraph.
options.feedback: El error gramatical en 'are visit' es claro.

questions.explanation:
Cuando describís tendencias que están cambiando (como el aumento de turistas en Salta), usás el presente continuo. El error acá es que faltó el "-ing" en el verbo principal después del "are". Debe ser "are visiting".

---

questions.statement: In many novels, authors use the "Narrative Present" to describe past events as if they were happening now. Why would an author choose this?
questions.context: Un análisis literario de una novela que usa el "presente narrativo".

options.text: Because they forgot the past tense rules.
options.feedback: Es una elección estilística deliberada, no un error gramatical.

options.text: To make the story feel distant and old.
options.feedback: El presente suele acercar la acción al lector, no alejarla.

options.text: To create a sense of immediacy and make the reader feel part of the scene.
options.feedback: ¡Excelente! El presente narrativo hace que la historia se sienta más viva y urgente.

options.text: Because English doesn't have enough past tenses.
options.feedback: El inglés tiene muchos tiempos de pasado; el presente se usa por estilo.

questions.explanation:
A veces, en los libros o cuando contás un chiste o una anécdota, usás el presente para que parezca que está pasando ahora mismo. "Then, the man walks into the room...". Esto se llama presente narrativo y sirve para que el que escucha o lee se sienta más metido en la historia.

---

questions.statement: Which auxiliary verb is used to form the Past Perfect tense?
questions.context: A student in Bogotá is learning about verb tenses in English class.

options.feedback: Incorrect. "Have" is used for present perfect (I have seen).
Incorrect. These are used for past continuous (I was going).
Correct. Past Perfect is formed with "had" + past participle (I had seen).
Incorrect. "Did" is used for simple past questions (Did you see?).

questions.explanation:
The Past Perfect tense is formed with the auxiliary "had" followed by the past participle of the main verb. It describes an action that happened before another past action. Example: "She had finished her homework before dinner."

---

questions.statement: What is the basic structure of the passive voice in English?
questions.context: A teacher explains the passive voice structure to students in Medellín.

options.feedback: Incorrect. That's the active voice structure.

options.text: Subject + to be + past participle (+ by agent)
options.feedback: Correct. Passive: "The cake was eaten (by Maria)." The object of the active sentence becomes the subject.
Incorrect. That's past perfect, not passive.
Incorrect. That's future simple.

questions.explanation:
The passive voice changes the focus from who does the action (agent) to the action itself. Structure: subject + form of "to be" + past participle. Example: "The letter was written by Juan." The agent (Juan) can be omitted.

---

questions.statement: What happened first according to this sentence?
questions.context: Read the sentence: "When the teacher arrived, the students had already finished the exam."

options.feedback: Incorrect. The past perfect ("had finished") indicates the earlier action.
Correct. Past perfect signals the action that happened first. The teacher's arrival (simple past) happened later.

options.text: Both happened at the same time
options.feedback: Incorrect. Past perfect indicates one action before another.

options.text: The teacher arrived before the students finished
options.feedback: Incorrect. That would use simple past for both actions.

questions.explanation:
Past Perfect (had + past participle) is used to show which of two past actions happened first. The action in Past Perfect happened before the action in Simple Past. Think of it as "the past of the past."

---

questions.statement: What is the main focus of this passive sentence?
questions.context: Read: "Coffee is grown in Colombia."

options.text: The people who grow the coffee
options.feedback: Incorrect. The agent is not mentioned.

options.text: The coffee itself (what happens to it)
options.feedback: Correct. The passive voice focuses on the action and the receiver of the action, not the doer.
Incorrect. The sentence states a fact, not a process.
Incorrect. Farmers are not mentioned.

questions.explanation:
The passive voice is used when the agent (doer) is unknown, obvious, or unimportant. "Coffee is grown in Colombia" focuses on the product (coffee), not on who grows it. The agent "by farmers" could be added but is unnecessary.

---

questions.statement: Choose the correct Past Perfect form.
questions.context: A student needs to complete: "She ___ (already / eat) lunch when I arrived."

options.feedback: Incorrect. Simple past doesn't show the sequence clearly.
Incorrect. Present perfect connects to present, not to another past action.
Correct. Past perfect shows that the eating happened before the arrival.
Incorrect. Past continuous suggests the actions overlapped.

questions.explanation:
When two actions happened in the past and we need to show which happened first, use Past Perfect for the earlier action. Key: "already" often signals past perfect in these contexts.

---

questions.statement: Complete the sentence in passive voice: "The new metro line ___ (build) by next year."
questions.context: A student in Cali writes about the Bogotá Metro project.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Active voice, not passive.
Incorrect. "Build" is not the correct past participle ("built").
Correct. Future passive: will + be + past participle (built).
Incorrect. Active voice in present perfect.

questions.explanation:
The passive voice can be formed in different tenses. Future passive: will + be + past participle. Example: "The new hospital will be opened in 2025." We don't need to say who will open it.

---

questions.statement: What does this sentence tell us about Shakira's career?
questions.context: Read the text: "Shakira had already released several albums before she became famous worldwide."

options.text: She became famous first, then released albums
options.feedback: Incorrect. The past perfect shows the albums came first.

options.text: She released albums after becoming famous
options.feedback: Incorrect. That would use simple past for both.

options.text: She released albums before becoming famous worldwide
options.feedback: Correct. "Had already released" happened before "became famous."

options.text: She became famous at the same time as releasing albums
options.feedback: Incorrect. Past perfect indicates a clear sequence.

questions.explanation:
This authentic context shows how Past Perfect is used in real biographical texts. Shakira's early albums (past perfect) happened before her worldwide fame (simple past).

---

questions.statement: Choose the correct passive form: "The peace agreement ___ (sign) in 2016."
questions.context: A student writes about the 2016 Peace Agreement in Colombia.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Active voice, and the agreement didn't sign itself.
Incorrect. Present passive; the event is in the past.
Correct. Past passive: was + past participle (signed). The agreement was signed by the government and the FARC.
Incorrect. Active voice in present perfect.

questions.explanation:
The past passive (was/were + past participle) is very common in historical descriptions. "The peace agreement was signed in 2016." We focus on the event, not on who signed it (though the agent can be added with "by").

---

questions.statement: What does this sentence imply about the sequence of events?
questions.context: Read: "By the time the rescue team arrived, the hikers had already found shelter in a cave."

options.text: The rescue team found shelter first
options.feedback: Incorrect. The team arrived later.

options.text: The hikers were looking for shelter when the team arrived
options.feedback: Incorrect. They had already found it.

options.text: The hikers found shelter, and THEN the rescue team arrived
options.feedback: Correct. Past perfect (had found) indicates the earlier action.

options.text: The rescue team arrived and immediately found shelter
options.feedback: Incorrect. The sequence is reversed.

questions.explanation:
"By the time" is a common time expression used with Past Perfect. It shows that one action was completed before another action started. The earlier action (had found) uses past perfect; the later action (arrived) uses simple past.

---

questions.statement: Change to passive voice: "The committee selected the winners last night."
questions.context: A news report about the Cartagena Film Festival.

options.text: The winners selected the committee last night
options.feedback: Incorrect. The meaning is reversed.

options.text: The winners were select by the committee
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Select" is not the past participle; it's "selected."

options.text: The winners were selected by the committee last night
options.feedback: Correct. Object (winners) becomes subject, "were" + past participle (selected) + agent (by the committee).

options.text: The committee was selected by the winners
options.feedback: Incorrect. The agent and subject are reversed.

questions.explanation:
To change active to passive: 1) Object becomes subject, 2) Add appropriate form of "to be," 3) Main verb in past participle, 4) Add "by + agent" if needed. Active: "The committee (subject) selected (verb) the winners (object)."

questions.statement: What does the negative Past Perfect form express here?
questions.context: A student reads: "He hadn't visited his hometown in ten years before he went back for the festival."

options.text: He visited his hometown many times
options.feedback: Incorrect. The sentence says he hadn't visited.

options.text: The last visit was more than ten years before the festival visit
options.feedback: Correct. Past perfect negative shows an action that didn't happen before another past action.

options.text: He never visited his hometown at all
options.feedback: Incorrect. The sentence doesn't say "never" generally, just not in the ten years before the festival.

options.text: He visited his hometown during the festival
options.feedback: Incorrect. The visit happened at the festival.

questions.explanation:
Negative Past Perfect (hadn't + past participle) shows that an action was NOT completed before another past action. It's useful for expressing regret or surprise: "I hadn't realized how much the city had changed."

---

questions.statement: Why does this text use the passive voice?
questions.context: Read the text about Colombian coffee: "Coffee is exported to over 90 countries. It is enjoyed by millions of people around the world."

options.text: Because the writer doesn't know who exports coffee
options.feedback: Possibly, but there's a better reason.

options.text: Because the focus is on the coffee itself (the product), not on who exports it. The agents (farmers, exporters) are less important than the fact.
options.feedback: Correct. Passive voice is used to focus on the action/subject rather than the agent.

options.text: Because the writer made a grammatical mistake
options.feedback: Incorrect. The passive voice is used intentionally.

options.text: Because English doesn't have an active voice for exports
options.feedback: Incorrect. English has both voices.

questions.explanation:
Texts about products, processes, and general facts often use the passive voice to focus on the subject. In coffee advertising, the focus is on the coffee's quality and global reach, not on individual producers.

questions.statement: Which tense is correct and why?
questions.context:
A student must choose between two tenses for this sentence:
"Sofia ___ (visit) Cartagena before, so she knew the best restaurants."

options.text: Visited - simple past, because the visit is in the past
options.feedback: Incorrect. Simple past suggests the visit was recent but doesn't establish the sequence clearly.

options.text: Had visited - past perfect, because the visit happened before she knew the restaurants. The sentence shows a clear sequence of two past events.
options.feedback: Correct. Past perfect clarifies which action happened first.

options.text: Has visited - present perfect, because it's connected to the present
options.feedback: Incorrect. The main clause is in simple past (knew).

options.text: Was visiting - past continuous, because it was in progress
options.feedback: Incorrect. Past continuous doesn't fit here.

questions.explanation:
Choose Past Perfect when you need to make clear that an action happened before another past action. If the sequence is obvious from context (e.g., with "after" or "before"), simple past can sometimes work, but past perfect is more precise.

questions.statement: This sentence uses passive voice in past perfect. What is its meaning?
questions.context: A student finds this sentence in a textbook: "The bridge had been built before the road was inaugurated."

options.feedback: Incorrect. Past perfect passive ("had been built") shows the bridge came first.

options.text: The bridge was built, and then the road was inaugurated
options.feedback: Correct. "Had been built" (past perfect passive) happened before "was inaugurated" (simple past passive).

options.text: Both happened at exactly the same time
options.feedback: Incorrect. Past perfect indicates a clear sequence.
Incorrect. The sentence says it was built.

questions.explanation:
Past perfect passive: had + been + past participle. This combines the past perfect (sequence) with the passive voice (focus on the action). Example: "The project had been completed before the deadline."

questions.statement: Which paragraph correctly uses both structures?
questions.context: A student needs to write a short paragraph combining past perfect and passive voice about the Gold Museum (Museo del Oro) in Bogotá.

options.text: "The Gold Museum opens in 1939. Many tourists visit it every year."
options.feedback: Incorrect. No past perfect or passive voice used.

options.text: "The Gold Museum was opening when the government had decided to create it."
options.feedback: Incorrect. Incorrect verb forms.

options.text: "The Gold Museum was founded in 1939. Before it opened, many gold pieces had been collected by archaeologists. Today, the museum is visited by thousands of tourists every year."
options.feedback: Correct. Uses passive (was founded, is visited), past perfect passive (had been collected), and shows correct sequence.

options.text: "The Gold Museum had been opening before the tourists visited."
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Had been opening" is incorrect - we need the past participle "opened" for passive.

questions.explanation:
Combining past perfect and passive voice allows for sophisticated expression: "had been collected" shows action before another past event, and "was founded" / "is visited" show appropriate passive forms in different tenses.

questions.statement: Which auxiliary verb is used to form the present perfect tense in English?
questions.context: Teacher María is explaining the present perfect tense to her 9th grade students at a school in Bogotá.

options.feedback: Incorrect. "do/does" are auxiliary verbs for the present simple in questions and negatives.
Correct. The present perfect is formed with the auxiliary "have" (or "has" for third person singular) + past participle.
Incorrect. "will" is an auxiliary verb used for the future tense.
Incorrect. "be" is used for continuous tenses (present continuous) and passive voice.

questions.explanation:
The present perfect tense connects the past with the present. Form: subject + have/has + past participle (+ complement). Example: "I have visited the Gold Museum in Bogotá." It is used for experiences, changes, and actions that started in the past and continue.

questions.statement: What is the correct structure for a first conditional sentence?
questions.context: In a classroom in Medellín, students are learning about conditional sentences.

options.text: If + present simple, will + base verb
options.feedback: Correct. First conditional: If + present simple (condition), will + base verb (result). Example: "If it rains, I will stay home."

options.text: If + past simple, would + base verb
options.feedback: Incorrect. That is the structure for the second conditional (unreal present situations).

options.text: If + will + base verb, present simple
options.feedback: Incorrect. The "will" clause cannot be in the "if" clause.

options.text: If + have + past participle, will + past simple
options.feedback: Incorrect. This combination is not a standard conditional structure in English.

questions.explanation:
The first conditional expresses a real possibility in the future. The "if" clause (condition) uses the present simple, while the main clause (result) uses "will" + base verb. Example: "If you study hard, you will pass the exam."

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly uses the comparative form of an adjective?
questions.context: Students at a school in Cali are learning about comparative adjectives.

options.text: Cartagena is more hot than Bogotá.
options.feedback: Incorrect. For one-syllable adjectives, "more" is not used. The correct form is "hotter" (double the last consonant).
Incorrect. The correct conjunction is "than", not "that".

options.text: The Amazon River is longer than the Magdalena River.
options.feedback: Correct. "Longer" is the correct comparative form of "long" (short adjective + -er).

options.text: The Sierra Nevada is the most high mountain in Colombia.
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is a superlative form (most + adjective), not comparative. Also, "high" → "highest", not "most high".

questions.explanation:
Comparative adjectives compare two things. Short adjectives (1 syllable) add -er: long → longer, tall → taller. Adjectives ending in consonant-vowel-consonant double the last letter: big → bigger. Long adjectives (2+ syllables) use "more": beautiful → more beautiful.

questions.statement: Which sentence uses the present perfect tense CORRECTLY to talk about an experience?
questions.context: At a language school in Bucaramanga, a teacher explains the difference between present perfect and simple past.

options.text: I have go to Cartagena last year.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "last year" is a specific past time, so simple past should be used: "I went to Cartagena last year."

options.text: I went to the Tayrona Park.
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is simple past, not present perfect.

options.text: I have visited the Museo del Oro in Bogotá.
options.feedback: Correct. Present perfect is used for experiences without specifying exactly when they happened.

options.text: I have visited the Museo del Oro yesterday.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "yesterday" is a specific past time, so simple past is needed: "I visited the Museo del Oro yesterday."

questions.explanation:
Present perfect is used for: 1) life experiences (no specific time), 2) changes over time, 3) actions that started in the past and continue. Simple past is for completed actions at a specific past time. "Have visited" is correct for a general experience.

questions.statement: Complete the sentence with the correct comparative form: "Medellín is _________ (modern) than it was 20 years ago."
questions.context: A student in Barranquilla is writing a paragraph about her favorite Colombian cities.

options.feedback: Incorrect. "Modern" has two syllables and does not take -er. The correct form is "more modern".
Correct. "Modern" has two syllables, so we use "more + adjective" for the comparative.
Incorrect. This is the superlative form, used to compare three or more things.
Incorrect. "-est" is for superlatives, not comparatives.

questions.explanation:
For two-syllable adjectives that do not end in -y, we use "more" + adjective for the comparative. Medellín is more modern than it was before. For one-syllable adjectives, we add -er: "taller", "shorter".

questions.statement: Choose the correct first conditional sentence: "If the weather is nice this weekend, we _________ to the beach."
questions.context: Carlos is talking about his weekend plans with his friend in Santa Marta.

options.feedback: Incorrect. After "will", the base form of the verb must be used: "will go".
Incorrect. The main clause needs "will + base verb" in first conditional.
Correct. "If + present simple, will + base verb" is the correct first conditional structure.
Incorrect. "would go" is used in second conditional (unreal situations), not first conditional (real possibility).

questions.explanation:
First conditional expresses a real possibility. If the condition is met (nice weather), the result will happen (going to the beach). The main clause uses "will" + base verb. Carlos might actually go to the beach if the weather is good.

questions.statement: Complete Ana's sentence: "I _________ (never / try) traditional Colombian sancocho."
questions.context: Ana is telling her classmates about her life experiences during an English class in Popayán.

options.feedback: Incorrect. The word order should be "have never tried" with the auxiliary "have" before "never".
Incorrect. After "have", the past participle form "tried" is needed, not the base form "try".
Correct. Present perfect: have + never + past participle. "Never" goes between the auxiliary and the main verb.
Incorrect. "Never" with simple past uses "did not ever try" or just "never tried". The present perfect requires "have/has + past participle".

questions.explanation:
Adverbs like "never", "ever", "already", and "yet" go between "have/has" and the past participle. "I have never tried sancocho" means Ana hasn't had this experience in her life so far.

questions.statement: Choose the correct superlative: "Mariana Pajón is one of _________ (successful) Colombian athletes in history."
questions.context: Students at a sports competition in Cali are comparing the Colombian athletes.

options.feedback: Correct. "Successful" is a long adjective; superlative uses "the most + adjective".
Incorrect. "-est" is only used for short adjectives. "Successful" needs "the most".
Incorrect. Superlatives need the definite article "the": "the most successful".
Incorrect. "More" is for comparatives (comparing two things), not superlatives.

questions.explanation:
Superlative adjectives are used to compare one thing with all others in a group. Long adjectives (2+ syllables): the most + adjective. Short adjectives: the + adjective + -est. Examples: the most beautiful, the tallest, the most important.

questions.statement: Read the two sentences. Which one is CORRECT?
questions.context: In an English exam in Bogotá, students must identify the correct use of present perfect vs. simple past.

options.text: "Yesterday, I have visited the Salt Cathedral of Zipaquirá."
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Yesterday" is a specific past time, so simple past is required: "I visited the Salt Cathedral yesterday."

options.text: "I have already visited the Salt Cathedral of Zipaquirá twice."
options.feedback: Correct. "Already" is used with present perfect to talk about completed experiences without a specific time.

options.text: "I have visited the Salt Cathedral last month."
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Last month" is a specific past time expression; use simple past: "I visited the Salt Cathedral last month."

options.text: "I didn't have visited the Salt Cathedral yet."
options.feedback: Incorrect. Negation in present perfect: "I haven't visited the Salt Cathedral yet." "Didn't" is for simple past.

questions.explanation:
Key difference: present perfect does NOT use specific past time expressions (yesterday, last week, in 2020). It uses unspecific time expressions: already, ever, never, yet, before. Simple past uses specific time expressions.

questions.statement: What is the error in the sentence "If I will have time, I will visit the Cocora Valley"?
questions.context: A student writes: "If I will have time, I will visit the Cocora Valley." The teacher says the sentence has a grammatical error.

options.text: The sentence is correct. No error.
options.feedback: Incorrect. There IS an error in the sentence.
Incorrect. "will visit" is correct in the main clause. The error is in the "if" clause.

options.text: "will have" should be "have" because in the first conditional, the "if" clause uses present simple, not "will".
options.feedback: Correct. The "if" clause must use present simple: "If I have time, I will visit the Cocora Valley."

options.text: "If" should be removed and replaced with "When".
options.feedback: Incorrect. The conjunction "if" is correct; the error is the verb tense.

questions.explanation:
A common mistake in first conditional is putting "will" in the "if" clause. The rule: "if" clause = present simple; main clause = will + base verb. The correction: "If I have time, I will visit the Cocora Valley." Never use "will" after "if" in first conditional.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that CORRECTLY uses the superlative form.
questions.context: A group of students from Bogotá are comparing different regions of Colombia for a school project.

options.text: The Amazon rainforest is the most largest region in Colombia.
options.feedback: Incorrect. We cannot use "most" and "-est" together. "Largest" alone is the superlative.

options.text: The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta is the highest coastal mountain in the world.
options.feedback: Correct. "Highest" is the correct superlative form of "high" (short adjective + -est).

options.text: The Pacific coast is more rainy than the Caribbean coast.
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is a comparative (comparing two things), not a superlative.

options.text: The most cold department in Colombia is Nariño.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Cold" is a short adjective; the superlative is "coldest", not "most cold".

questions.explanation:
For short adjectives (1 syllable), add -est: high → highest, cold → coldest. For long adjectives (2+ syllables), use "the most": the most beautiful. Never combine both: NOT "the most highest". "More" is for comparatives (between two things), not superlatives.

questions.statement: Why is this sentence grammatically incorrect?
questions.context: A student says: "I have gone to the Galerías mall last Sunday."

options.text: "have gone" is not a valid verb form.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "have gone" is a valid present perfect form.
Incorrect. The name of the mall is not the grammatical issue.

options.text: "Last Sunday" is a specific past time, so we should use simple past ("I went") instead of present perfect ("I have gone").
options.feedback: Correct. Present perfect cannot be used with specific past time expressions.
Incorrect. The combination of present perfect with a specific past time is incorrect.

questions.explanation:
Present perfect is incompatible with specific time references like "last Sunday", "yesterday", "in 2023", "two days ago". Correct: "I went to the Galerías mall last Sunday" (simple past) or "I have been to the Galerías mall" (present perfect, no specific time).

questions.context: In a debate at school, a student claims: "The first conditional and the second conditional have the same meaning."

options.text: Yes, both conditionals express the same type of situation.
options.feedback: Incorrect. They express very different types of situations.

options.text: No, the first conditional uses "will" while the second uses "would", but they mean the same thing.
options.feedback: Incorrect. They differ not only in form but also in meaning.

options.text: No, the first conditional expresses a real or probable future situation, while the second conditional expresses an unreal or hypothetical present situation.
options.feedback: Correct. The meaning is fundamentally different between real (1st) and unreal (2nd) conditionals.

options.text: Yes, because both use "if" at the beginning.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Using "if" does not make them equivalent in meaning.

questions.explanation:
First conditional: "If I study, I will pass" = real possibility, high probability. Second conditional: "If I studied, I would pass" = unreal or hypothetical situation, low probability or impossible. The key difference is REAL (1st) vs. UNREAL (2nd) situations.

questions.statement: How many errors are there in this paragraph regarding comparative/superlative usage?
questions.context: A teacher asks students to identify the error in the following paragraph: "Bogotá is the most big city in Colombia. It has more people than Medellín. However, Medellín is the more beautiful city in my opinion."

options.text: No errors. The paragraph is correct.
options.feedback: Incorrect. There are errors in the paragraph.

options.text: Two errors. "Most big" should be "biggest", and "more beautiful" should be "the most beautiful".
options.feedback: Correct. "Big" is a short adjective (biggest), and "beautiful" needs "the most" for superlative.

options.text: One error. "Most big" should be "biggest". "More beautiful" is correct.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "More beautiful" is a comparative form, but the context requires a superlative ("the most beautiful").
Incorrect. "More people than Medellín" is correct (comparative between two cities). Only the superlative forms are wrong.

questions.explanation:
Error 1: "most big" → "biggest" (short adjective takes -est). Error 2: "more beautiful" → "the most beautiful" (superlative needs "the most" for long adjectives, and it compares Medellín with ALL Colombian cities, not just one other).

questions.statement:
Read the following student paragraph and identify which sentence contains a grammar error:

"Colombia is a beautiful country. I have visited the Coffee Region last year. The Caribbean coast is hotter than the Andes. If you visit Colombia, you will have an amazing experience."
questions.context: A student writes a short paragraph about Colombian culture and makes several mistakes.

options.feedback: Incorrect. This sentence is grammatically correct with correct subject-verb agreement.

options.text: "I have visited the Coffee Region last year."
options.feedback: Correct. This sentence incorrectly uses present perfect with a specific past time expression ("last year"). It should be: "I visited the Coffee Region last year."

options.text: "The Caribbean coast is hotter than the Andes."
options.feedback: Incorrect. This sentence correctly uses the comparative form "hotter" (short adjective, double the t).

options.text: "If you visit Colombia, you will have an amazing experience."
options.feedback: Incorrect. This sentence correctly uses the first conditional: if + present simple, will + base verb.

The error is in sentence B. Present perfect ("have visited") cannot be used with specific past time expressions like "last year", "yesterday", or "in 2020". The correct version uses simple past: "I visited the Coffee Region last year." Present perfect would be correct without the specific time: "I have visited the Coffee Region."

questions.statement: Complete the sentence with the correct past perfect form: "By the time we arrived, the movie _____."
questions.context: A student is reviewing past perfect tense formation.

options.feedback: Incorrect. This is simple past, but the action happened before another past action.

Correct. The past perfect (had + past participle) is used to show that an action was completed before another past action. "By the time we arrived" establishes the later past moment, so "had started" is the correct tense.
Incorrect. Present perfect cannot be used when the reference time is in the past.
Incorrect. Past continuous does not express completion before another past action.

questions.explanation:
Past perfect (had + past participle) is used to express an action that happened before another action or time in the past. The earlier action takes past perfect; the later action takes simple past.

---

questions.statement: What is the correct grammatical structure for a Type 2 (second) conditional?
questions.context: In class, the teacher explains the structure of type 2 conditionals.

options.text: If + present simple + will + base verb
options.feedback: Incorrect. That's the first conditional, used for real/possible situations.

options.text: If + past simple + would + base verb
options.feedback: Correct. The second conditional (If + past simple, would + infinitive) is used for unreal or improbable situations in the present or future. Example: "If I had more time, I would travel the world."

options.text: If + past perfect + would have + past participle
options.feedback: Incorrect. That's the third conditional, used for unreal past situations.

options.text: If + present perfect + will + base verb
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is not a standard conditional structure.

questions.explanation:
The second conditional expresses hypothetical, unreal, or improbable situations. The past simple in the if-clause does not refer to past time but to an unreal present situation.

---

questions.statement: If someone says "I am tired," how do you report this in the past?
questions.context: A student needs to transform direct speech into reported speech.

options.feedback: Incorrect. When the reporting verb is in the past, the verb tense usually shifts back.

options.text: She said she was being tired
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Was being" is past continuous, which doesn't fit here.
Correct. In reported speech, when the reporting verb is past (said), the present tense "am" shifts to past "was." This is called backshift of tenses.

options.text: She said she has been tired
options.feedback: Incorrect. Present perfect is not the correct backshift for present simple.

questions.explanation:
In reported speech, when the reporting verb is in the past tense (said, told, asked), verbs shift back: present → past, past → past perfect, etc. "I am" → "she was."

---

questions.statement: What is the difference between "If it rains, I will stay home" (1st conditional) and "If it rained, I would stay home" (2nd conditional)?
questions.context: Students analyze the difference between first and second conditionals.

options.text: There is no difference; they mean the same thing
options.feedback: Incorrect. They express different levels of probability.

options.text: The first is about the past; the second is about the future
options.feedback: Incorrect. The first conditional is about the future.

options.text: The first conditional expresses a real possibility (it might rain), while the second conditional expresses an unreal or improbable situation (I don't expect it to rain)
options.feedback: Correct. The first conditional (if + present, will) is used for real, possible situations. The second conditional (if + past, would) is for hypothetical or unlikely situations. The past tense in the second conditional signals unreality, not past time.

options.text: The first is polite; the second is impolite
options.feedback: Incorrect. Politeness is not the grammatical distinction here.

questions.explanation:
The choice of conditional structure reflects how probable the speaker considers the condition. The second conditional often expresses dreams, wishes, or situations contrary to current reality: "If I won the lottery, I would buy a house."

questions.statement: Choose the correct option: "When I _____ (arrive) at the party, Maria _____ (leave) already."
questions.context: A student writes a paragraph using past perfect and simple past correctly.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Both in simple past doesn't clarify which happened first.
Incorrect. Both in past perfect is unnecessary. Only the earlier action needs past perfect.
Correct. The arrival (arrived) is in simple past, and Maria's departure (had left) happened before that, so it takes past perfect. This clearly shows the sequence: first Maria left, then I arrived.
Incorrect. Present tenses are not appropriate for a past context.

questions.explanation:
Past perfect establishes the order of two past events. The earlier event takes past perfect; the later event takes simple past. This avoids ambiguity about which event happened first.

questions.statement: How do you correctly report this question: "Do you like coffee?" she asked.
questions.context: Students practice transforming direct questions to reported speech.

options.text: She asked if do I like coffee
options.feedback: Incorrect. Reported questions do not use auxiliary "do" in the same way.

options.text: She asked if I liked coffee
options.feedback: Correct. In reported yes/no questions, use "if" or "whether." The verb "like" shifts back (liked), and the word order changes from question to statement (I liked, not do I like).

options.text: She asked if I like coffee
options.feedback: Incorrect. Without backshift, it's not fully correct reported speech when the reporting verb is past.

options.text: She asked that I like coffee
options.feedback: Incorrect. "That" is not used to introduce reported yes/no questions. Use "if" or "whether."

questions.explanation:
Reporting questions requires: 1) changing question word order to statement word order, 2) backshifting the tense, 3) using "if"/"whether" for yes/no questions, and 4) removing the question mark.

---

questions.statement: "Clean your room!" my mom told me. In reported speech:
questions.context: A student must transform a direct command into reported speech.

options.text: My mom told me that clean my room
options.feedback: Incorrect. The structure is missing "to."

options.text: My mom told me to clean my room
options.feedback: Correct. Reported commands use tell + person + to + infinitive. The imperative "clean" becomes "to clean."

options.text: My mom told me that I cleaned my room
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is a statement, not a reported command.

options.text: My mom told me cleaning my room
options.feedback: Incorrect. The gerund is not used for reported commands.

questions.explanation:
Reporting commands: tell + object + to + infinitive. Example: "Sit down" → He told me to sit down. For negative commands: "Don't run" → He told me not to run.

---

questions.statement: How many past perfect verbs are in the text?
questions.context: Students read a short paragraph and must identify all examples of past perfect.

options.feedback: Incorrect. There are more.
Correct. All three verbs use "had + past participle": had finished, had eaten, hadn't arrived. Each indicates an action completed before another past action or time.
Incorrect. "Hadn't arrived" is also past perfect (negative form).
Incorrect. "Watched" and "was" are simple past.

questions.explanation:
Past perfect can be affirmative (had + past participle), negative (hadn't + past participle), and interrogative (had + subject + past participle). It always refers to the "past of a past."

questions.statement: "If I were you, I would apologize." What does this sentence imply?
questions.context: Students analyze the meaning of a second conditional sentence.

options.feedback: Incorrect. The second conditional implies unreality.

options.text: The speaker is giving advice, but the listener is not the speaker. The "were" shows this is an unreal situation because the speaker cannot be the listener
options.feedback: Correct. "If I were you" (using "were" for all persons, not "was") is a fixed expression for giving advice. It implies: "I can't be you, but if it were possible, my recommendation would be to apologize." The subjunctive "were" signals unreality.
Incorrect. The second conditional expresses hypothetical situations.

options.text: The speaker wants to become the listener
options.feedback: Incorrect. It's a rhetorical device for giving advice, not a literal wish.

questions.explanation:
"Were" in the second conditional is the subjunctive form. Use "were" for all subjects (I, he, she, it) in unreal conditionals: "If she were taller, she would play basketball" (not "was").

---

questions.statement: She said, "I will call you tomorrow." Which reported speech version is correct?
questions.context: Students analyze reported speech transformations for time expressions.

options.text: She said she will call me tomorrow
options.feedback: Incorrect. Without backshift, this is direct speech punctuation removed, not true reported speech.

options.text: She said she would call me the next day
options.feedback: Correct. In reported speech, "will" becomes "would" and "tomorrow" becomes "the next day" or "the following day." This reflects both tense backshift and time expression shift.

options.text: She said she would call me tomorrow
options.feedback: Partially correct. The tense backshift is correct (will → would), but "tomorrow" should shift to "the next day" for formal reported speech, although it's common in informal contexts.

options.text: She said she called me the next day
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Called" changes the meaning entirely (past action, not future intention).

questions.explanation:
In reported speech, time expressions also shift: now → then, today → that day, yesterday → the day before, tomorrow → the next day, here → there.

---

questions.statement: Why does the text use past perfect in the first two sentences but simple past in the third?
questions.context: Students read a paragraph mixing past perfect and simple past.

options.feedback: Incorrect. The tense choice is intentional.

options.text: Past perfect is used for background information (experiences before the main narrative moment), while simple past advances the narrative (the announcement happened at the narrative time)
options.feedback: Correct. Past perfect sets the background: her previous experience (had never flown) and actions completed before (had booked). Simple past moves the story forward (announced). This is a typical narrative pattern: past perfect for background, simple past for main events.

options.text: Simple past is always wrong in narratives
options.feedback: Incorrect. Simple past is the default tense for narrative.

options.text: Past perfect should be used everywhere in past narratives
options.feedback: Incorrect. Overusing past perfect makes the text awkward. It's used only to clarify sequence.

questions.explanation:
In narrative writing, past perfect provides background information or "earlier past" actions. Simple past advances the main storyline. This alternation creates clarity about the sequence of events.

questions.statement: Complete: "If I _____ (live) on the coast, I _____ (go) to the beach every day."
questions.context: A student must complete a second conditional sentence about Colombia.

options.feedback: Incorrect. First conditional for real possibility, but the context is hypothetical.
Incorrect. Mixed conditional: if-clause is second conditional, but result clause is first conditional, which is not standard.
Correct. Second conditional: If + past simple (lived), would + base verb (would go). The speaker imagines living on the coast (hypothetical, not true now).
Incorrect. Third conditional for past unreal situations. Here the context is present/future imaginary.

questions.explanation:
Remember the pattern: Second Conditional = If + past simple, would + infinitive. It expresses imaginary or unlikely present/future situations.

---

questions.statement: What grammatical transformations occurred in this reported speech example?
questions.context: Students compare direct and reported speech in a dialogue.

options.feedback: Incorrect. Multiple changes occurred.

options.text: Three changes: pronoun (I → she), verb tense shift (didn't see → hadn't seen / past → past perfect), and time expression (yesterday → the day before)
options.feedback: Correct. 1) Pronoun shifts: I → she. 2) Backshift: simple past "didn't see" → past perfect "hadn't seen." 3) Deixis shift: "yesterday" (relative to speaker's now) → "the day before" (relative to reporting moment).
Incorrect. Pronouns and time expressions also change.

options.text: No changes are needed because the tense is already past
options.feedback: Incorrect. Simple past shifts to past perfect in reported speech.

questions.explanation:
Reported speech requires multiple simultaneous adjustments: person (pronouns), tense (backshift), time/place references (deixis), and word order (for questions). Each change depends on the context and the reporting verb tense.

---

questions.statement: Which sentence is better and why? "When I arrived, the train left" vs. "When I arrived, the train had left."
questions.context: A student evaluates whether the past perfect is necessary in a given sentence.

options.text: Both are equally correct and mean the same thing
options.feedback: Incorrect. They imply different sequences.

options.text: The first sentence is better because it is simpler
options.feedback: Incorrect. Simpler is not always clearer or more correct.

options.text: The second sentence is better because it clearly shows that the train left BEFORE I arrived. The first sentence is ambiguous: it could mean the train left at the moment I arrived or before
options.feedback: Correct. "When I arrived, the train had left" (past perfect) clearly shows the departure preceded the arrival. "When I arrived, the train left" (both simple past) is ambiguous — did it leave as I arrived or before? The past perfect removes ambiguity.
Incorrect. Both are grammatically correct; one is clearer.

questions.explanation:
Using past perfect when it's needed avoids ambiguity. Good writers use it to clarify the sequence of events. In speech, context often clarifies, but in writing, the past perfect is essential for precision.

---

questions.statement: A student writes: "If the government would invest more in education, the country develops faster." What is wrong with this sentence, and how should it be corrected?
questions.context: Students evaluate the use of conditionals in argumentative writing.

options.feedback: Incorrect. There is a grammatical error in the conditional structure.

options.text: It should be: "If the government invests more in education, the country will develop faster" (first conditional for real possibility)
options.feedback: This is a correct form but changing the meaning to a real conditional. Let me see the other options.

options.text: It should be: "If the government invested more in education, the country would develop faster" (second conditional for hypothetical situation). The original incorrectly mixes "would" in the if-clause and uses present simple in the result clause.
options.feedback: Correct. The original has two errors: 1) using "would" in the if-clause (except for polite requests), and 2) using present simple in the result clause. The standard second conditional is: If + past simple (invested), would + base verb (would develop).

options.text: It should be: "If the government had invested more in education, the country would develop faster"
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is a mixed conditional (third + second) that implies the investment didn't happen in the past.

questions.explanation:
Common mistakes with conditionals: putting "would" in the if-clause (✗ If I would have time), or mixing structures inconsistently. Remember: "would" only goes in the result clause, not the if-clause.
